deep.reconstruction:
Setting (my interpretation, since the page gives no context): m = a+ib is a Gaussian modulus, presumably a primary Gaussian prime. k = A+iB is a Gaussian integer prime to m (Gauss writes the imaginary part as a Fraktur B). Square brackets [w] mean the 'Gaussian integer part', i.e. floor of the real part plus i times floor of the imaginary part. (Whether Gauss meant floor or nearest integer is my inference.)

Step 1 (on the page). For each z = x+iy in a fixed region Δ (a triangle, labelled 'Δ o'), form
  [ (1+i) z k / m ] = α + iβ.
The region presumably holds a fixed fraction of a residue system mod m, i.e. a 'half/quarter system' in the sense of Gauss's lemma.

Step 2 (on the page). 'summirt alle −(α ■ β)^2, indem für x+iy alle im Δ o liegenden Werthe gesetzt werden.' One sums an expression −(α ? β)^2 over all z in Δ. The operator between α and β is blotted out; α−β or α+β is most likely. Presumably the sum taken mod 4 (or the parity of its parts) gives the exponent of i in the biquadratic character (k/m)_4. This is a Gaussian-integer analogue of the floor-sum (Gauss lemma / Eisenstein lattice-point) form of the quadratic character.

Step 3 (on the page). 'Die einzelnen (1+i)(x+iy) sind [struck word]' followed by
  (1+i)(a+ib) − (ξ+iη).
The image reads (1+i)(a+b), which is most likely a slip or omitted i for (a+ib). The multiples (1+i)z are thus written as complements with respect to (1+i)m, with ξ+iη running over a complementary or reflected set of points.

Step 4 (on the page). Substituting gives
  (1+i) z k / m = (1+i)k − (ξ+iη) k / m,
so the bracket becomes
  [ (1+i)(A+iB) − (ξ+iη)(A+iB)/(a+ib) ].

Implicit next step (mine). (1+i)k is a Gaussian integer, and for w with non-integral real and imaginary parts,
  [N − w] = N − [w] − (1+i).
Hence
  α + iβ = (1+i)k − (1+i) − [ (ξ+iη) k / m ].
This relates the bracket sum over Δ to the bracket sum over the reflected region. It is the standard symmetry device used in lattice-point proofs of reciprocity.

The page breaks off here.
errors: (1+i)(a+b) should almost certainly read (1+i)(a+ib), since the complement must be taken relative to (1+i)m. This is a writing slip or a faint i.
The operator in −(α ■ β)^2 is obliterated, so the summand cannot be fixed with certainty.
Δ is not defined on this page, so the claimed role of the sum cannot be verified from this page alone.

results.what: Character of k modulo m expressed through a sum over a region Δ of a function of the Gaussian integer parts [(1+i) z k / m].
results.modern_name: Gauss-lemma / Eisenstein lattice-point type criterion for the biquadratic residue character
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (lemma for quadratic residues, 1808; biquadratic theory 1828–32); Eisenstein (1844) for the published lattice-point/lemma proof of biquadratic reciprocity

results.what: Reflection z -> (1+i)m − (ξ+iη) and the identity [N − w] = N − [w] − (1+i) for Gaussian integer N.
results.modern_name: complementary-point (symmetry) argument in floor-sum reciprocity proofs

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's unpublished work on biquadratic reciprocity, including Gauss-lemma style approaches, is partly known from Werke II/X. This fragment is a sketch of an Eisenstein-type floor-sum approach in Z[i]. It is notable as a detail but is consistent with known Nachlass material, and it is too fragmentary to establish a new result.
